extracted.intended_audience: advanced students, mathematicians and physicists studying classical mechanics (readers of Newton's Principia)
extracted.subtask_description: Statements and construction-methods (propositions, problems, corollaries, examples) about motions of bodies under various centripetal forces: apsidal motion of near-circular orbits, motion on surfaces, rolling/cycloid constructions, and isochronous pendula. Includes formulas relating force laws to orbital geometry and timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 3 (ellipses concentric, relation of forces for mobile/stationary ellipses)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a fixed ellipse VPK has its center at the center of forces C, and a similar, equal, concentric moving ellipse vpk is supposed, with 2R as the semiparameter and 2T the transverse semiaxis, and the angle VCp is always to angle VCP as G to F, then the forces by which bodies in the fixed and moving ellipse may be revolved in equal times are respectively Fq·A ÷ T^3 and Fq·A ÷ T^3 + {RGq - RFq} ÷ A^3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives how to combine the base centripetal term Fq·A ÷ T^3 with the additional difference term {RGq - RFq} ÷ A^3 for the moving ellipse; follows from prior corollaries and similarity of shapes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 4 (universal formula for centripetal force in given altitude)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the maximum altitude CV is T and the radius of curvature at V equals R, and the centripetal force at V is Fq ÷ Tq (denoted {Fq ÷ Tq} at V), then at a general point P of altitude A the centripetal force required to give the same motion circularly is X + {VRGq - VRFq} ÷ A^3, where X denotes the centripetal force at P coming from the motion in the fixed orbit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a universal expression to get the centripetal force at any altitude A by adding a correction term proportional to 1/A^3 involving R, G, F; is a generalization of previous corollaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 5 (altering angular motion to obtain new stationary orbits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given the motion of a body in any orbit under a given centripetal force, the angular motion about the centre of forces may be increased or diminished in a given ratio, and thereby new stationary orbits (in which bodies revolve under the new centripetal forces) can be found.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows how to modify angular speed to determine other stationary orbits; practical method indicated by preceding constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 6 (force producing given tangential curve is ∝ 1/(Cp)^3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If from a point on the axis CV a perpendicular VP is erected and PC is joined and Cp is taken equal to Cp forming angle VCp to VCP in a given ratio, then the centripetal force by which a body can be made to move in the curve Vpk (touched perpetually at p) is reciprocally proportional to the cube of the altitude Cp (i.e. ∝ 1 / Cp^3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives a geometric construction linking an altitude (distance from centre) and the reciprocal-cube law required to produce the specified curved trajectory; follows from decomposition of forces and earlier propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XLV / Problem XXXI (apsidal motion for nearly circular orbs)
rubrics_metrics.description: For orbs which approach very nearly to circles, determine the motions of their apsides (i.e., how the line of apsides advances) by representing the orbit-describing centripetal forces as series in the altitude A (replace A by T - X) and comparing numerators after expansion; the method reduces the problem to algebraic series manipulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solve arithmetically: express centripetal force as fraction with denominator A^3, substitute A = T - X, expand numerator in series, collate terms with known RGq - RFq + TFq - Fq·X etc., then take limits as orbit becomes circular (T and R → equal, X → 0) to obtain ratios governing apsidal advance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example 1 (uniform centripetal force → apsidal angle 180/√3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the centripetal force is uniform (i.e., ∝ A^0 so that numerator equals T^3 - 3T^2 X + 3T X^2 - X^3 over A^3), then in the limit of nearly circular orbit G:F :: 1:√3, hence the angle between VCp and VCP is in ratio 1:√3; a body moving in such an almost-circular orbit will go from apse to opposite apse with central angle 180/√3 (~103°55'), repeating perpetually.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows a concrete computed apsidal advance for uniform (constant) centripetal force by taking limiting ratios as orbit tends to circular; explicit numeric angle given and geometric interpretation of motion between apsides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example 2 (force ∝ A^{n-3} → apsidal angle 180/√n)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the centripetal force is proportional to A^{n-3} (i.e., effective numerator A^n), then in the near-circular limit G:F :: 1:√n, so the angle between successive apsides in the nearly circular orbit equals 180/√n degrees. Special cases: n=4 (force ∝ A) gives 90°; n=2 (force ∝ 1/A) gives ~127°17'; n=1/4 (extreme fractional power) yields 360° (full revolution between apsides).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General formula linking power-law dependence of centripetal force on distance to apsidal advance; many qualitative consequences follow (if force decays faster than inverse-cube, body may fall to centre, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Example 3 (linear combination bA^m + cA^n → general apsidal formula)
rubrics_metrics.description: If centripetal force ∝ (bA^m + cA^n)/A^3, then in the near-circular limit G^2 : F^2 :: (bT^{m-1} + cT^{n-1}) : (mbT^{m-1} + ncT^{n-1}); with T normalized to 1 this simplifies to G^2 : F^2 :: b + c : mb + nc, hence G:F = 1 : sqrt((mb+nc)/(b+c)). Consequently the angle between apsides = 180·sqrt((b + c)/(mb + nc)). If the combination is bA^m - cA^n analogous formulas apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives a method to handle mixed power-law centripetal forces by series expansion and term-by-term comparison; reduces to simple algebraic ratio when the maximal altitude is set to unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 1 to Prop. XLV (recover force law from apsidal motion)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the total angular motion between returns to the same apse bears ratio m:n to 360°, and altitude is A, then the centripetal force is proportional to A^{(nn÷mm) - 3}. Thus measuring apsidal advance (m:n) lets one infer the power-law exponent of the centripetal force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides inversion: from observed apsidal precession per revolution infer the distance-dependence exponent of the force; many numeric examples are given illustrating possible exponents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 2 to Prop. XLV (effect of adding/removing an external force on apsidal motion)
rubrics_metrics.description: If in an elliptical motion produced by a primary force ∝ 1/A^2 (inverse-square) an external force (e.g. subtracting cA) is added or removed, the resulting effective centripetal law becomes (A - cA^4)/A^3 and the apsidal angle is altered accordingly; example shows angle = 180·sqrt{(1 - c)/(1 - 4c)} and numerical estimate of apsidal advance per revolution when c is small.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows how small external perturbing forces change apsidal advance; provides explicit numeric computation for a small perturbation c to demonstrate practical effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XLVI / Problem XXXII (reduce motion on a plane offset from centre to planar problem)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given any centripetal force with given force centre S and a given plane at distance SC from S, for a body leaving P along a given line with given speed, the motion in that plane can be found by projecting the centripetal force SV onto components ST and TV where SV is proportional to the actual centripetal force; the ST component (normal to the plane) does not alter motion within the plane and the TV component acts like a planar centripetal force toward point C enabling reduction to the planar free-space problem about C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: choose SV proportional to given centripetal force, resolve into ST normal to plane and TV lying in plane; ignore ST for in-plane motion and treat TV as centripetal force toward C; apply Prop. XLII to find trajectory and velocities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XLVII / Theor. XV (Hookean central force → ellipses and equal periods)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the centripetal force is proportional to the distance of the body from the centre (i.e., linear restoring force), then bodies moving in any plane under that force describe ellipses and perform their revolutions in equal times; they may also oscillate back and forth in straight lines through the centre, completing equal periods forward and back.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows that a linear (Hooke-type) central force yields closed elliptical orbits with isochronous periods; reasoning uses proportionality and earlier corollaries on equivalence of forces in different planes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholium (motion on surfaces via revolved planar curves)
rubrics_metrics.description: Motion of bodies on curved surfaces generated by revolving planar curves about axes through the centre of forces reduces to motion in the generating planar curves: bodies moving obliquely on such surfaces ascend and descend and their motion is equivalent to motion in planes passing through the axis, so it suffices to consider motion in those generating plane curves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides conceptual reduction for motion on surfaces of revolution: analyze planar sections through axis to deduce full-surface dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XLVIII / Theor. XVI (length of curve traced by point on wheel rolling outside a sphere)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a wheel rolls on a globe externally at right angles and progresses along a great circle while rotating so that arc AB of the globe equals arc PB of the wheel, then the length of the curvilinear path traced by a fixed point P on the wheel's rim from the first contact to the next contact equals (2·CE)/(CB) times the versine (sinus versus) of the half-arc of the wheel that contacted in that time; in symbols AP : (2·sin(½PB)) :: (2·CE) : CB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric construction and limiting-similarity argument relate infinitesimal increments of the traced curve to wheel and globe geometry; yields formula for cycloidal-type curves generated on a sphere by rolling wheel externally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XLIX / Theor. XVII (length when wheel rolls inside a concave globe)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the wheel rolls inside a concave globe (intrinsically at right angles) and rotates so that arcs correspond as before, then the length of the curve traced by a rim point P over the interval is to twice the versine of the half-arc as the difference of the diameters of globe and wheel is to the semidiameter of the globe; i.e., the same relation but with diameters difference replacing sum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogous limiting-similarity geometric derivation to Prop. XLVIII; yields relation for the interior cycloid (trochoid inside the sphere).

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 1 to Prop. XLIX (relation of half-cycloid arc to rim/path segment)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a complete (external) cycloid ASL is bisected at S, then the length PS (from contact point P to S) is to the rim-segment VP (which equals double the sin of arc ½BP for wheel radius ½BV) as 2CE is to CB; gives proportion between cycloid part and wheel geometry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct consequence of Prop. XLVIII geometry connecting cycloid arc lengths to wheel and globe diameters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 2 to Prop. XLIX (semiperimeter of cycloid equals a straight line proportion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The length of the half-perimeter of the cycloid AS equals a straight line which is to the wheel's diameter BV as 2CE is to CB; provides a simple relation to compute half-perimeter from geometrical elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful practical relation: cycloid semiperimeter computed from wheel and globe radii.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 3 to Prop. XLIX (semiperimeter proportional to rectangle BEC)
rubrics_metrics.description: Thus the half-perimeter length is proportional to rectangle BEC when the globe's semiradius is given; gives alternative proportional statement linking cycloid length with rectangle under geometry of wheel and globe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Another geometric proportionality useful for practical calculation when globe semidiameter is known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. L / Problem XXXIII (construct a pendulum that oscillates in a given cycloid)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an inner cycloid QRS on a globe and its bisected arc, construct an external semicycloid AQ, AS tangent to the outer globe so that a pendulum of length AR equal to AR (constructed as CA:CO :: CO:CR etc.) will oscillate inside the given cycloid QRS; the construction ensures that as the string wraps on/off the semicycloid the suspended bob moves along the desired inner cycloid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical geometric construction using homothetic circles and semicycloids: choose point A such that CA:CO :: CO:CR, construct semicycloids and suspend a bob on a string of length AR — the motion will be confined to the given cycloid QRS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary to Prop. L (equality of the string AR to half-cycloid arc APS)
rubrics_metrics.description: The string length AR equals the half-arc APS of the constructed semicycloid; this equality underlies the construction of the cycloidal pendulum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirms the geometric equivalence used to make the pendulum follow the given cycloid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LI / Theor. XVIII (linear central force + cycloidal constraint → isochronism)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a centripetal force tending to the globe centre C is everywhere proportional to the distance CT, and if that single force (acting alone) causes the body to oscillate on the cycloid QRS as previously constructed, then any unequal oscillations (different amplitude) will nevertheless take equal times: all oscillations are isochronous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof decomposes the central force into components along tangent and normal; acceleration along cycloid is proportional to the cycloid arc, hence acceleration and the remaining path persist in fixed proportion leading to equal times for unequal amplitudes. This establishes isochronism of the cycloidal pendulum under linear central force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LII / Problem XXXIV (determine pendulum velocities and times at positions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a cycloid with semicircle construction and a central force proportional to distance from that centre, the velocities of a pendulum at any point and the times for full and partial oscillations can be determined: velocity ratios are as sqrt(SR^2 - TR^2) : SR and times are proportional to corresponding semicircle arc ratios.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mapping between the cycloid and a semicircle (via equal arc correspondence) and earlier propositions (Prop. XXXVIII etc.) to compute times and velocities; provides explicit formulae in terms of geometric elements SR, TR, LI, GK etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LIII / Problem XXXV (force law to make oscillations in any given curve isochronous)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given any curved path STRQ whose axis passes through the centre of forces C, take at any point T the tangent TX and choose TY equal to the arc TR; then if the centripetal force is everywhere proportional to the perpendicular TZ (from the point of the curve to the axis), the oscillations of a body constrained to that curve will be isochronous (all amplitudes take equal time).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: choose TY equal to the arc to be described and make the centripetal force proportional to TZ; decomposition of force into components shows accelerations are proportional to the arcs to be described, yielding synchronous description of parts and hence equal total times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 1 to Prop. LIII (circular arc + vertical parallel force with given ratio → equal single oscillation times)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a pendulum suspended from A describes a circular arc STRQ and is urged by a downward force (parallel) which relates to the uniform gravity such that the applied force corresponds (via similar triangles) to arc TR : arc TN (its sinus), then single oscillations have equal times (isochronous singles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies Prop. LIII to the circular-arc special case, expressing the required downward auxiliary force in terms of the arc and its sine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 2 to Prop. LIII (clock design: combine mechanism force with gravity to achieve isochronism)
rubrics_metrics.description: In clock mechanisms, if the force the mechanism adds to a pendulum can be composed with gravity so that the total downward force at every position equals the rectangle under arc TR and radius AR to the sine TN, then the pendulum's oscillations will be isochronous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescribes how to shape the driving force applied by a clock so as to preserve (or enforce) isochronism by matching the geometric-force relation given by Prop. LIII.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LIV / Problem XXXVI (compute descent/ascent times along any curved path under any centripetal force)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a curved line STtR lying in a plane through the centre and a given centripetal law, divide CS into many equal parts, construct corresponding circles and intercepts; using Proposition XXXIX to get velocities at heights, the time to traverse an infinitesimal element Tt is proportional to its length divided by velocity, hence proportional to an ordinate DN (the secant of angle tTC). Integrating these ordinated rectangles (area SNDS) gives the time of descent from S to any point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives an integral-like geometric quadrature method to obtain times of descent/ascent by reducing the time element to an area under a constructed curve SNDS; requires knowledge of quadratures of given curved figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LV / Theor. XIX (area described by a parallel is proportional to time on curved surface motion)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a body moves on a curved surface whose axis passes through the centre of forces, and from the body a perpendicular is dropped to the axis and a parallel equal to it is drawn through a fixed point O on the axis, then the area AOP swept by the radius OP is proportional to the time taken by the body to move from the initial point to P. In other words, the area described about a fixed axis-parallel radius is proportional to time for motion on such surfaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof decomposes the centripetal force into components resolving the normal and tangential effects; only components parallel to the designated plane affect motion in that plane, and the constructed area AOP (with radius OP) accumulates in proportion to time, generalizing the planar areal-time relation to motions on curved surfaces.
